DSA-101, one interview question every day. Today: LeetCode 1, Two Sum. One notebook turns five hundred billion checks into one million steps.

Save this for your interview. Send it to the friend who still writes two loops.

scenes.vo: An interviewer asked me Two Sum. I wrote two loops. He smiled. Not a good smile.
Here is the question. A list of numbers, and a target. Find the two numbers that add up to the target, and return their positions. Two plus seven is nine. So: zero, one.
My first answer: try every pair. Two loops. It works! But with a million numbers, that is five hundred billion checks. At a billion a second, eight minutes. His coffee went cold.
Pause the video. Try to beat it. I will wait. Hint: you only need one notebook.
Picture a wedding gate. Guests walk in one by one, each wearing a number. The host keeps a notebook of everyone already inside.
For every new guest, ask: who is my partner? That is target minus my number. Is the partner in the notebook? Yes: done. No: write me down, and wait for the next guest.

That is the whole algorithm. Eight lines. The notebook is a dictionary called seen. For each number, work out the partner. If the partner is in seen, return both positions. Otherwise, write this number down.
Let us run it. Guest one is two. The partner needed is seven. The notebook is empty. So, write two down.
Guest two is seven. The partner needed is two. Is two in the notebook? Yes, at position zero! Answer: zero, one. Done in two steps.
One trap. Three and three, target six. Always check the notebook first, then write. Do it the other way, and a number pairs with itself. Wrong answer, confident face.
Now the maths. Five hundred billion checks became one million steps. Eight minutes became one millisecond. Same answer. Just one notebook.
With this answer, the interviewer would have said: next question. That is a good smile.
This notebook has a proper name: a hash map. It finds anything in one step. Remember this trick. It appears everywhere.
Notes for your revision. Time: order n. Space: order n. Trade a little memory for a lot of speed. Amazon candidates report this one.
Quick quiz. The numbers are already sorted. Which is better: a hash map, or two pointers? Comment A or B.

data.question: Sorted numbers. Which is better?
data.why: Two pointers needs no extra memory.
